title: HTTP Status Codes: The Ones You'll Actually Use
description: A practical reference for the HTTP status codes that show up constantly in day-to-day API development, grouped by what they mean for the client.
bodyHtml:
HTTP status codes fall into five classes by their first digit: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error. Most day-to-day work only touches a couple dozen of the ~60 registered codes.

2xx — Success

CodeMeaningWhen to use it
200 OKGeneric successGET/PUT/PATCH that returns a body
201 CreatedResource createdSuccessful POST that creates something
204 No ContentSuccess, no bodySuccessful DELETE, or PUT with nothing to return

3xx — Redirection

CodeMeaning
301Permanent redirect — search engines transfer ranking to the new URL
302Temporary redirect — original URL stays authoritative
304Not Modified — client's cached copy is still valid

4xx — Client error

CodeMeaningCommon cause
400Bad RequestMalformed syntax or invalid parameters
401UnauthorizedMissing or invalid authentication
403ForbiddenAuthenticated, but not allowed
404Not FoundResource doesn't exist
409ConflictRequest conflicts with current state (e.g. duplicate unique field)
422Unprocessable EntityWell-formed request, but semantically invalid data
429Too Many RequestsRate limit exceeded

5xx — Server error

CodeMeaning
500Internal Server Error — generic failure, check server logs
502Bad Gateway — upstream server sent an invalid response
503Service Unavailable — server overloaded or down for maintenance
504Gateway Timeout — upstream server took too long to respond

401 vs 403, quickly

401 means "we don't know who you are" (fix: log in / send valid credentials). 403 means "we know who you are, and you're not allowed" (fix: nothing the client can do without different permissions).
